content_html_sanitized:
Ed. Note: Jacques Chirac's government was the most rabidly prohibitionist in Europe. Gabriel Nahas is even his principle "drugs" policy adviser, which meant an insane obsession with marijuana. President Chirac was the major source of pressure on the Dutch to change their policies.

The rate of cannabis use in France is actually higher than it is in Holland, and most of the cannabis in France is hashish from Morocco. (In France the enforcement of the cannabis laws fall most heavily on the young North African Moslems, who have an appalling rate of unemployment.) But facts never had much influence on prohibitionists.Chirac even announced that he was going to close the French border with the Netherlands. No, don't look at the map. France does not have a border with the Netherlands. Chirac, however, did keep border checks with Belgium and Luxembourg, which do. But he did not keep them with Germany, which also does. This means that if someone wants to smuggle from Holland to France, he must go all the way around Luxembourg.

Under the French system power is divided between the Prime Minister and the President. Prior to the last elections, Chirac's party controlled both positions, but lost control of the parliament to the Socialists. When the Socialist Jospin was campaigning for Prime Minister he promised to decriminalize cannabis, but he went back on his word after he won, partially in response to the Stalinist communists. (It might be easier to learn French than to try to make sense of this.) However, the pressure was taken off the Dutch and --little by little -- the "good guys" among the more liberal Socialists are chipping away at the cannabis laws. That a newspaper like Le Monde would report something like this is important. The Paris paper, Liberation has been consistently anti-prohibitionist, but most of the French establishment has been cravenly prohibitionist.

Several years ago I attended a trial in Paris at which Dr. Grinspoon was a witness for the defense of a man with AIDS who had been caught with a small amount of hashish. The court found him guilty, but refused to impose any penalty. This was considered a victory at the time. Things are advancing.

LOBBY GROWS FOR 'MEDICINAL MARIJUANA'
From Le Monde ("The New York Times" of France)
January 13, 1998
By Laurence Follea

THE Movement for Controlled Legalisation (MLC), which advocates the sale of narcotics under state control, has just asked the French health minister, Bernard Kouchner, to authorise the import of 10kg of cannabis for therapeutic use.The jurists of the MLC base their arguments on articles of the public health code that give the health authorities the right to authorise the import and use of narcotics for medical or scientific research. The Swiss company Valchanvre has offered to supply, free, 10kg of its Walliser Queen variety of cannabis for the MLC's experiment. The use of cannabis as a medicine was recently legalised in California. Germany is considering prescribing drugs containing the active ingredient of cannabis for Aids sufferers, and the Netherlands is looking into the possibility of "medical marijuana" being paid for by social security.

Ten patients who are MLC members and have medical certificates showing that they suffer from such ailments as epilepsy, glaucoma, tinnitus, headaches or HIV infection, have written to Kouchner describing the relief they derive from cannabis. Some of them have been in trouble with the law because of their practice. Eugène Gaudet, a doctor in the southern town of Millau, has certified that when one of his patients, a 20-year-old epileptic, smoked cannabis he was able to relax: "The fact that he has smoked such products has created no incident likely to jeopardise the harmonious family environment or his ability to work normally."

Janine Cervoni, who has been treating a young HIV-positive patient at the Lariboisière Hospital in Paris, stresses the role that cannabis plays as a "psychological support" for her patient. Pierre Lembeye, a Paris psychiatrist, has noted a genuine therapeutic affect on one of his patients, who suffers from hearing disorders. "The patient has tried cannabis since 1977. He has an immediate feeling of relaxation and an appreciable reduction in his hearing disorders.

"These isolated medical observations do not constitute scientific proof, and the virtues of cannabis have yet to be confirmed. In a recent editorial, however, the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine came out in favour of the "compassionate" use of such products by terminal patients. Kouchner himself is in favour of such an approach. But it remains to be seen what action he will take in response to the MLC's request.
